paragraphs: Giving a language model several attempts can increase the chance that at least one answer succeeds. This paper studies how that chance changes as the number of attempts grows. It focuses on coverage, also called pass@k, which measures success somewhere among the attempts rather than the quality of a single answer.

The authors propose a simple statistical model built around memorization to explain the shape of inference scaling curves observed on reasoning tasks. Within this framework, they define an inference loss that decreases according to a power law as more trials are made. They also connect that behavior to prompting costs, relating the benefit of additional attempts to the resources those attempts require.

Experiments with a simple generative model produce coverage curves consistent with the framework’s predictions in a controlled setting. This agreement supports the proposed explanation without establishing that it describes every language model or task. The contribution is a tractable starting point for connecting repeated inference with scaling laws concerning training data, model size, and computation.
icml-2025-a-simple-model-of-inference-sc.tldr: A memorization-based statistical model explains how repeated inference attempts can improve coverage and connects their gains to prompting costs.

paragraphs: Face recognition models learn numerical representations of faces using training objectives centered on identity. Nevertheless, the resulting representation space can also organize itself around other properties. This paper observes geometric patterns at multiple scales associated with interpretable facial attributes, such as hair color, and image attributes, such as contrast.

The authors develop a geometric approach for describing how strongly a model’s representations depend on particular attributes or remain unchanged when those attributes vary. They introduce an alignment metric inspired by physics to make this relationship measurable. This shifts attention from whether identities can be distinguished to how additional properties shape the representations used for that distinction.

The metric is evaluated on controlled, simplified models and commonly used face recognition models fine-tuned with synthetic data targeting specific attributes. The findings show that invariance varies across attributes: a model may be relatively insensitive to some properties while responding more strongly to others. These differences provide a more interpretable account of model strengths and weaknesses, even when identity is the only information explicitly emphasized by the training labels.
icml-2025-attributes-shape-the-embedding.tldr: A geometric metric reveals how facial and image attributes shape face recognition embeddings despite identity-focused training.

paragraphs: A time series model may process several channels whose numerical inputs look identical even though the channels have different characteristics. Channel identifiability is the ability to preserve that distinction. Without it, a model can produce identical outputs for identical inputs while overlooking which channel supplied them. This paper makes that ability an explicit modeling concern.

The proposed Channel Normalization gives each channel its own affine transformation parameters, allowing channel identity to influence the processed values. Adaptive Channel Normalization extends this idea by adjusting parameters according to the input time series. Prototypical Channel Normalization instead uses learnable prototypes, making the approach applicable when the number of channels is unknown or changes across datasets.

The authors apply these methods to several time series models and report significant gains for models both with and without existing channel identifiability. They also analyze the approach through information theory. The results suggest that representing channel distinctions can improve forecasting-related modeling beyond merely adding a missing identifier, while the prototype variant makes the idea usable in time series foundation models.
icml-2025-channel-normalization-for-time.tldr: Channel-specific normalization and its adaptive variants improve time series models by preserving distinctions between input channels.

paragraphs: Split inference divides a model’s computation between an edge device and a cloud server, allowing large models to operate with limited local resources. The server receives an intermediate representation rather than necessarily receiving the original input. This paper examines how much image information can still be recovered from those representations in vision foundation models.

DRAG uses a pretrained latent diffusion model as a source of prior knowledge about images. Guided diffusion repeatedly refines a reconstruction within that learned image prior, using the intermediate representation to help produce an image resembling the original. The approach brings the generative knowledge of a large pretrained model into a reconstruction problem previously studied mainly with smaller convolutional classifiers.

The reported experiments show substantial qualitative and quantitative improvements over existing reconstruction attacks, including attacks on representations from deep layers of a vision foundation model. These findings indicate that moving computation deeper into a model does not, in the evaluated settings, prevent substantial visual information from being recovered. The privacy implication is that split inference for large models needs protections that account for powerful generative reconstruction methods.
icml-2025-drag-data-reconstruction-attac.tldr: DRAG uses guided diffusion to reconstruct images from vision foundation models’ intermediate representations, exposing privacy risks in split inference.

paragraphs: Predicting student performance requires understanding how students interact with learning material as well as how their responses change over time. EduLLM addresses interactions and their meaning by combining language-model features with a structured representation of students, multiple-choice questions, and response records. The goal is more accurate prediction to support personalized education.

Its structural component, FraS-HNN, represents students and questions as nodes in a signed hypergraph. Response records become positive and negative hyperedges, providing a way to encode interactions involving multiple nodes. The model uses framelet-based low-pass and high-pass filters to extract information at different frequencies, capturing complementary patterns within this structure.

EduLLM combines these hypergraph representations with fine-grained semantic features derived from large language models. This gives the predictor access to both the organization of response interactions and information about their meaning. Experiments on multiple educational datasets report significant improvements over state-of-the-art baselines. The stated findings support the value of integrating semantic and structural information for student performance prediction, beyond approaches that primarily emphasize the temporal sequence of past responses.
icml-2025-edullm-leveraging-large-langua.tldr: EduLLM combines language-model semantic features with signed hypergraph learning to improve student performance prediction.

paragraphs: Distributed training often performs several local optimization steps before combining updates across machines. This reduces communication, but creates inner and outer optimization processes that must both handle noisy gradients. The paper studies heavy-tailed noise, where unusually large fluctuations can make training difficult and gradient variance may be unbounded.

TailOPT combines adaptive optimization with new clipping techniques for this setting. The authors establish convergence guarantees that allow local updates and potentially unbounded gradient variance. A particular version, Bi²Clip, clips individual gradient coordinates from above and below at both optimization levels. It aims to capture benefits associated with adaptive methods such as Adam without maintaining or communicating additional gradient statistics.

This design links robustness to noisy updates with practical limits on memory and communication. Experiments across several tasks and models report better performance than state-of-the-art methods alongside greater efficiency. The theoretical contribution concerns convergence in the heavy-tailed setting, while the empirical contribution shows that the framework and its economical clipping variant can also be useful in the evaluated training workloads.
icml-2025-efficient-distributed-optimiza.tldr: TailOPT uses adaptive optimization and clipping to make distributed training efficient and provably convergent under heavy-tailed gradient noise.

paragraphs: Graph Transformers can attend across a graph, but their effectiveness depends on how graph structure is represented for that attention mechanism. This paper develops structural encodings based on random walks. The central idea is to describe a graph through the long-term behavior of movement along its connections, giving the Transformer richer information about topology.

The authors adapt Green and Martin kernels for use in learning systems while retaining their mathematical foundations. These kernels summarize long-term random-walk behavior and are designed to represent complicated structures, including non-aperiodic and directed acyclic substructures. Their role is to supply structural information that helps guide global attention rather than leaving the model to infer all graph organization from other inputs.

Evaluations on eight benchmark datasets report strong performance across different tasks, particularly in molecular and circuit applications. The authors attribute the gains to the encodings’ ability to capture intricate structural relationships. The findings support using mathematically grounded descriptions of graph connectivity as a practical source of inductive bias for Transformer-based graph learning.
icml-2025-from-theory-to-practice-rethin.tldr: Adapted Green and Martin kernels encode long-term random-walk structure to strengthen Graph Transformers across benchmark tasks.

paragraphs: Node embeddings summarize a node’s position and relationships in a graph as a vector. Methods such as node2vec can supply structural information when node features are absent or supplement features that already exist. Their usual limitation is that the graph, including test nodes, must be available during training, making later arrivals difficult to represent.

Inductive node2vec, or iN2V, addresses this with two connected changes. It modifies node2vec training to prepare the learned embeddings for extension, then uses a procedure after training to compute embeddings for previously unseen nodes. Preparing the original representations and extending them are therefore parts of the same approach, rather than treating new nodes as an unrelated embedding problem.

Experiments on several benchmark datasets report an average one-point improvement in node classification, with gains reaching six points depending on the dataset and number of unseen nodes. The method can create embeddings, enrich existing ones, and work with other embedding techniques. These results support its use as a plug-in way to carry structural node representations into settings where the graph expands beyond the nodes observed during training.
icml-2025-in2v-bringing-transductive-nod.tldr: iN2V adapts node2vec training and adds a post-training procedure to represent unseen nodes and improve node classification.

paragraphs: Predicting three-dimensional physical systems requires outputs that respond consistently when the spatial coordinate system changes. Geometric neural networks enforce this property, called equivariance, but can struggle to incorporate broader information. Language models offer access to such information, yet applying them directly does not guarantee the spatial behavior required for these predictions.

EquiLLM combines geometry-aware prompting, an equivariant encoder, a language model, and an equivariant adapter. The architecture assigns different responsibilities to these components. The language model processes invariant features under guidance from the prompt, while the encoder and adapter exclusively handle three-dimensional directional information. This arrangement integrates language-model capabilities with E(3)-equivariant processing.

Experiments report significant improvements over previous methods in molecular dynamics simulation, human motion simulation, and antibody design. The diversity of these applications suggests promising generalizability for the framework. Its main methodological contribution is the separation of invariant feature processing from directional processing, allowing broader information to contribute to predictions while the geometric components maintain the required transformation behavior.
icml-2025-large-language-geometry-model-.tldr: EquiLLM combines language-model feature processing with equivariant geometric modules to improve predictions for three-dimensional physical systems.

paragraphs: A deployed forecasting model receives a useful stream of feedback as new observations reveal what actually happened. Time series foundation models often remain fixed because updating these large models online is computationally expensive. Consequently, their forecasts may not adjust to the current characteristics of the data, even when recent feedback is available.

ELF introduces a lightweight way to use that feedback. It contains an ELF-Forecaster that learns the current data distribution and an ELF-Weighter that combines this forecaster’s predictions with those of the foundation model. Adaptation therefore happens through a smaller forecasting and weighting mechanism around the existing model, making new observations useful without requiring online learning of the foundation model itself.

The authors evaluate ELF alongside several recent foundation models on standard time series datasets and report improvements in every experiment they conduct. That consistency applies to the tested combinations of models and datasets. The findings show that an additional adaptive mechanism can make practical use of incoming feedback and improve forecasts from otherwise fixed foundation models.
icml-2025-lightweight-online-adaption-fo.tldr: ELF improves fixed foundation-model forecasts by combining them with a lightweight forecaster that learns from incoming data.

paragraphs: Multimodal systems must connect information across different kinds of input while retaining what makes each modality distinctive. The paper argues that learning primarily in the original token space can lead to modality collapse. M3-JEPA instead aligns modalities in a learned representation space, using a predictor to map input embeddings into the space of output embeddings.

The predictor is a multi-gate mixture of experts. Its gating mechanism separates information shared across modalities from information specific to each one, with an accompanying information-theoretic optimality result. Training combines contrastive and regularization losses and alternates gradient descent between different multimodal tasks. Together, these choices organize how the system shares information without treating every modality as interchangeable.

The reported experiments show state-of-the-art performance across different modalities and tasks, generalization to unseen datasets and domains, and computational efficiency during training and inference. These findings support latent-space prediction as a useful approach to multimodal alignment. The authors also suggest that the framework could provide a basis for open-world self-supervised learning, presenting that broader role as a possibility.
icml-2025-m3-jepa-multimodal-alignment-v.tldr: M3-JEPA aligns modalities through latent-space prediction and gated experts that separate shared information from modality-specific information.

paragraphs: Flow and diffusion models generate outputs through an inference trajectory, a sequence of states leading toward the final result. This paper asks whether the controls governing that trajectory can be made more flexible. It identifies two properties of simulation-based methods that conventional flow and diffusion approaches lack: freedom of dimensionality and adaptation to different inference trajectories.

The proposed Multidimensional Adaptive Coefficient, or MAC, is a plug-in module that expands conventional one-dimensional coefficients into multidimensional ones. It also allows adaptation specific to an inference trajectory. MAC learns through feedback from simulations using adversarial refinement, connecting the adjustment of these coefficients to the behavior of the generation process.

Experiments across several frameworks and datasets report improved generation quality with high training efficiency. The contribution is therefore both a module and a different focus for optimization: the paper directs attention toward adapting inference trajectories alongside designing the vector fields that guide generation. Its empirical findings support simulation-based refinement as a useful route to better outputs in the evaluated flow and diffusion systems.
icml-2025-multidimensional-adaptive-coef.tldr: MAC improves flow and diffusion generation by learning multidimensional coefficients that adapt to individual inference trajectories.

paragraphs: The 1-identification problem asks whether any option in a multi-armed bandit has an average reward at least as large as a known threshold. An algorithm samples the options and must either identify a qualifying option or conclude that none exists. Its answer must be correct with probability at least one minus a specified error tolerance.

The paper studies how many samples this decision requires. Earlier work had characterized the limiting, asymptotic sample complexity, while the finite-sample analysis remained unresolved. The authors introduce Sequential-Exploration-Exploitation, or SEE, and analyze its number of pulls without relying solely on behavior in an asymptotic limit. This makes the central question how efficiently the decision can be reached at finite confidence levels.

The resulting upper and lower bounds match up to a polynomial logarithmic factor, establishing near optimality in that qualified sense. Numerical results also indicate that SEE is effective compared with existing benchmarks. The contribution is a finite-sample theoretical account of this exploration problem, supported by numerical evidence, rather than an exact equality between the achievable and unavoidable sample counts.
icml-2025-near-optimal-non-asymptotic-sa.tldr: SEE solves threshold-based bandit identification with finite-sample complexity matching lower bounds up to a polynomial logarithmic factor.

paragraphs: Real-world image super-resolution uses generative models to produce higher-resolution images from degraded inputs. Multi-step diffusion can deliver strong results, but repeated sampling adds computation and latency. One-step methods reduce that burden, although their results can inherit weaknesses from the teacher model used during training, including visible artifacts.

FluxSR builds a one-step super-resolution method from the flow matching model FLUX.1-dev, using it as both teacher and base model. Flow Trajectory Distillation transfers a multi-step generation process into a single sampling step. The method also introduces TV-LPIPS, a perceptual loss intended to improve realism, and Attention Diversification Loss, which reduces token similarity inside the Transformer to address high-frequency artifacts.

The reported experiments show that FluxSR outperforms existing one-step diffusion-based methods for real-world super-resolution. The approach combines compression of the generation trajectory with objectives aimed at the visual problems that can remain after compression. Its findings support the usefulness of jointly addressing sampling efficiency, teacher quality, and artifact-related training behavior when building a fast super-resolution model.
icml-2025-one-diffusion-step-to-real-wor.tldr: FluxSR distills a flow matching model into one-step super-resolution and adds losses that improve realism and suppress high-frequency artifacts.

paragraphs: Quantum Hamiltonian Descent uses quantum dynamics, including tunneling, to move through difficult optimization landscapes and escape local traps. Its original formulation mainly uses function values. The paper identifies slow convergence relative to classical gradient methods and limited robustness on highly non-convex problems as challenges for this approach.

The authors propose incorporating gradient information into Quantum Hamiltonian Descent. Their motivation comes from high-resolution differential equations that help explain acceleration in classical optimization. Gradients provide information about how an objective changes, adding directional guidance to the quantum optimization process. The resulting method is called gradient-based QHD and is intended to improve both convergence and the chance of reaching a global solution.

Numerical simulations on challenging problem instances report faster convergence, a substantially greater likelihood of finding global solutions, and performance exceeding existing quantum and classical methods by at least an order of magnitude. These are findings from the simulated instances described in the abstract. The central contribution is showing how gradient information can strengthen a quantum optimization method whose original design relies primarily on objective values.
icml-2025-quantum-optimization-via-gradi.tldr: Adding gradient information to Quantum Hamiltonian Descent improves convergence and global-solution discovery in numerical simulations.

paragraphs: A degraded image or speech signal still contains information about the clean signal that produced it. Conditional diffusion models use the degraded observation during restoration, but a standard Gaussian starting distribution does not incorporate that information into the prior itself. RestoreGrad asks whether learning a more informative prior can make restoration better and more efficient.

The framework integrates a denoising diffusion model with a variational autoencoder and learns the prior jointly with the diffusion model. Correlations between degraded and clean signals help shape this starting distribution. The design therefore uses the observation both as conditioning information and as a source of information for the diffusion prior.

On speech and image restoration tasks, the authors report better restored-signal quality than existing diffusion baselines while requiring five to ten times fewer training steps to converge. They also report greater robustness when reducing inference sampling steps, with two to two-and-a-half times fewer steps. These findings connect a more informative learned prior to efficiency in both training and restoration, alongside improvements in output quality in the evaluated tasks.
icml-2025-restoregrad-signal-restoration.tldr: RestoreGrad jointly learns an observation-informed diffusion prior, improving restoration quality while reducing training and inference steps.

paragraphs: ReVISE trains a language model to examine its own reasoning and revise it when needed. The paper treats checking a reasoning process and correcting that process as two distinct capabilities that must work together. Its aim is an efficient self-correction framework in which the model’s own verification guides further reasoning.

Training follows a structured curriculum based on preference learning. The model learns self-verification and reasoning correction sequentially, using successful and failed reasoning paths to construct preference pairs. These paired examples provide training signals about better and worse reasoning behavior. Separating the learning stages is the proposed way to handle the difficulty of acquiring both capabilities efficiently.

At inference time, verification and correction can be combined repeatedly, allowing additional test-time computation to support further refinement. A confidence-aware decoding mechanism further enhances this process. Experiments on multiple reasoning tasks report efficient self-correction and significant reasoning improvements. The findings support teaching models how to evaluate and revise their reasoning as a practical route to gaining value from additional inference effort.
icml-2025-revise-learning-to-refine-at-t.tldr: ReVISE uses sequential preference training to teach language models to verify and correct their reasoning during inference.

paragraphs: Adversarial changes to graph structure can undermine a graph neural network’s predictions. Training one classifier to achieve both accuracy and robustness can entangle those objectives. This paper separates the defensive task by placing a dedicated purifier before the classifier, so that graph recovery and prediction are handled by different components.

The purifier, GPR-GAE, is a graph autoencoder trained through self-supervision. It uses multiple Generalized PageRank filters to capture different structural representations and adapt to graph structure in a data-driven way. Purification proceeds through multiple steps, which the authors use to improve recovery of the graph and resistance to structural perturbations.

Experiments across datasets and attack scenarios report state-of-the-art robustness. The purifier is presented as an independent, plug-in component for graph neural network classifiers. This matters because the defensive mechanism can be organized around cleaning the input graph, while the classifier retains its prediction role. The stated results support this separation as an effective approach to robustness in the evaluated settings, with the multiple filters and repeated purification providing its central structural tools.
icml-2025-self-supervised-adversarial-pu.tldr: GPR-GAE improves graph neural network robustness through a separate self-supervised purifier that repairs structurally perturbed inputs.

paragraphs: Hyper-relational knowledge graphs extend ordinary subject–relation–object facts with qualifiers that supply additional information. Their structure therefore includes relationships among entities, relations, facts, and qualifiers. This paper investigates how far representation learning can go when it thoroughly uses that structure, reporting that a purely structural method can achieve state-of-the-art link prediction performance.

The proposed method, MAYPL, learns initial representation vectors from graph structure. It then uses attentive message passing, computing messages at the fact level and aggregating them around both entities and relations. These steps keep the representations grounded entirely in structural information while allowing different parts of a hyper-relational fact to contribute to the learned vectors.

Because its learning is structure-driven, MAYPL can make inductive inferences involving new entities and relations. The authors report outperforming 40 knowledge graph completion methods across ten datasets, with different baselines compared on different datasets. The findings demonstrate the strength of structural representation learning in the tested tasks and show that careful handling of hyper-relational organization can support both completion and inference beyond previously observed entities and relations.
icml-2025-structure-is-all-you-need-stru.tldr: MAYPL learns entirely from hyper-relational graph structure, achieving strong link prediction and supporting inference on new entities and relations.

paragraphs: A language model can face a conflict between information stored in its parameters and information supplied in the current context. Earlier explanations assign separate attention heads to memory and context. This paper finds that influential heads can contribute to both simultaneously, a phenomenon the authors call superposition of contextual information and parametric memory.

Just Run Twice, or JuICE, uses this observation to intervene in attention at inference time. It identifies reliable attention heads and uses a dual-run procedure to reduce the effects of their mixed contributions. The intervention can steer the model toward either its parametric beliefs or contextual knowledge without fine-tuning. That flexibility addresses which information source the model follows when the sources disagree.

Experiments across eleven datasets and six model architectures report state-of-the-art performance and consistent improvements across domains and conflict types. The authors also provide a theoretical analysis of knowledge conflicts and superposition in attention heads. Together, the findings connect a revised account of attention-head behavior with a practical way to control knowledge preference during inference.
icml-2025-taming-knowledge-conflicts-in-.tldr: JuICE uses two inference runs and attention interventions to steer language models toward stored or contextual knowledge without fine-tuning.

paragraphs: CLIP represents images and text in a shared embedding space, but the geometry of that space is not fully understood. This paper finds that the two modalities occupy separate ellipsoid shells whose centers are displaced from the origin. The shells are linearly separable, revealing an organized geometric difference between image and text representations.

The authors explain how this structure can represent differing levels of uncertainty during contrastive training. Frequent concepts generate more false negatives, which increases uncertainty. They introduce conformity as the average cosine similarity between an instance and other instances in a representative dataset, providing a way to describe how closely a representation aligns with the surrounding collection.

The paper shows that conformity can be estimated accurately through cosine similarity with the mean vector for the modality, avoiding the need to calculate every pairwise comparison. It also finds that CLIP’s modality gap optimizes the matching of image and text conformity distributions. These results give the separation between modalities a functional interpretation tied to uncertainty and the statistical organization of the embedding space.
icml-2025-the-double-ellipsoid-geometry-.tldr: CLIP’s image and text embeddings form separate ellipsoid shells whose geometry relates to uncertainty and similarity distributions.

paragraphs: This paper looks for statistical patterns shared by real-world and synthetic datasets by treating data like a physical system. It examines eigenvalues of feature covariance matrices, which describe how variation is distributed across combinations of features. Tools from statistical physics and random matrix theory allow the authors to compare both broad spectral patterns and local eigenvalue behavior.

The findings distinguish uncorrelated Gaussian data from real-world data in their bulk eigenvalue power laws. Introducing long-range correlations into Gaussian data reproduces that power-law behavior. At the same time, all examined dataset types exhibit chaotic random-matrix universality. These shared statistics appear at sample sizes smaller than typical training sets and correlate with power-law convergence.

The authors also find a relationship between Shannon entropy and random-matrix structure, with fewer samples needed in strongly correlated datasets. Taken together, the observations suggest that natural-image Gram matrices may be approximated using Wishart random matrices with a simple covariance structure. Such an approximation could make rigorous analysis of neural network behavior more tractable while retaining important statistical features of natural data.
icml-2025-the-underlying-universal-stati.tldr: Covariance spectra reveal shared random-matrix structure across studied datasets and suggest simple correlated models for natural-image statistics.

paragraphs: Highly detailed image captions can include unsupported claims even when the model describes much of the image correctly. This paper finds that existing hallucination detectors struggle with such captions. The authors attribute the difficulty to multimodal models increasingly relying on their own generated text as captions grow longer, weakening the connection to the input image.

The proposed correction method uses collaboration between language models and multimodal language models to revise existing captions. The paper also introduces an evaluation framework and benchmark for detailed caption analysis, with factuality and coverage as evaluation concerns. This pairs a method for improving captions with tools for examining whether their claims are accurate and how thoroughly they describe the image.

Experiments show that the proposed evaluation aligns better with human factuality judgments than existing metrics. The correction approach significantly improves caption accuracy, including captions produced by GPT-4V, while current factuality-enhancement methods often fail in this setting. The paper also finds that visual question-answering performance may not correlate with detailed captioning ability, highlighting the need to evaluate this generation task directly.
icml-2025-toward-robust-hyper-detailed-i.tldr: Collaborating language and multimodal models improve detailed captions, while a new evaluation framework better matches human factuality judgments.

paragraphs: Counterfactual outcome estimation asks what an outcome would have been under a different circumstance. When observations vary across locations and over time, an estimator must account for both spatial and temporal attributes. This paper proposes a Transformer-based framework for that problem, addressing performance and generalization limitations associated with earlier classical statistical approaches.

The contribution combines a learned estimation framework with theoretical guarantees. Under assumptions described by the authors as mild, the estimator is consistent and asymptotically normal. Consistency concerns approaching the target as data increase, while asymptotic normality characterizes the limiting form of estimation error. These properties are conditional on the stated assumptions rather than automatic consequences of using a Transformer.

Simulation experiments report stronger estimation ability than baseline methods. The authors also apply the framework to real data concerning the causal effect of conflict on forest loss in Colombia. This application connects the estimator to a concrete spatial-temporal causal question. The abstract reports a valuable conclusion from that analysis without specifying the effect’s direction or size.
icml-2025-transformer-based-spatial-temp.tldr: A Transformer framework improves spatial-temporal counterfactual estimation in simulations and has consistency and asymptotic normality under stated assumptions.

paragraphs: This paper examines data quality across both pretraining and later model control. Its question is whether exposure to more toxic text during pretraining could make toxicity easier to remove afterward. That possibility depends on how the model represents toxicity internally, as well as how frequently the untreated model generates toxic output.

A toy experiment investigates how data composition affects representation geometry. Controlled experiments then train Olmo-1B models with different mixtures of clean and toxic data. As the toxic fraction increases, the authors find that toxicity has a less entangled linear representation. The base models generate more toxic text, but the corresponding internal feature is also easier to target for removal.

Evaluations on Toxigen and Real Toxicity Prompts show a better trade-off between reducing generated toxicity and preserving general capabilities when detoxification methods such as inference-time intervention are applied. The finding is conditional on considering that later intervention: more toxic pretraining data also worsens the untreated model’s toxicity. The broader implication is that useful training-data choices may depend on how pretraining and post-training are designed together.
icml-2025-when-bad-data-leads-to-good-mo.tldr: In controlled experiments, more toxic pretraining data makes base models more toxic but can improve the trade-off achieved by later detoxification.
